title: Price Zedu for buyers outside Nigeria, by Fri 27 Nov
description: Pricing shows naira only: ₦0 and ₦20K per month. A school in Ghana, Kenya or the UK sees a currency it cannot pay in and no statement about whether it can buy at all. Decide the currency and payment position, then publish it next to the price rather than in a footnote. Work: confirm which currencies can be billed, what happens to the price when the exchange rate moves, and which payment method a buyer outside Nigeria uses. Then write the wording for the pricing page and the sign-up path, and check it against what the billing screens actually accept.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Decide whether a foreign price is a conversion or a price, and write the rule down
acceptedWorkstreams.description: Converting naira at today's rate produces a price that changes weekly and a number a buyer distrusts. Setting a separate price produces two prices that can drift apart and a discount for one market. Neither is wrong; leaving it undecided is. Work: take the real plan prices, show both options with worked examples at three exchange rates, state what happens when the rate moves more than a set amount, and recommend one with the reason. Deliver the rule, the example table, and the sentence that will appear under the price so a buyer knows what they are being charged.

upvotes.reason: "Decide whether a foreign price is a conversion or a price, and write the rule down" has a defined audience and a clear done-state, and it addresses something the site does not currently say. it produces something checkable rather than an opinion, so the goal either moved or it did not.
A foreign price is either a conversion or a price. Writing the rule down stops the team making both decisions on different days.
Converting naira at the daily rate creates a price that changes weekly and a number buyers distrust; deciding the rule before the page prevents rework.
One written rule for foreign prices - FX source, rounding, review date - stops per-page improvisation and makes published prices auditable.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Find out what the billing provider can actually charge before writing any price
acceptedWorkstreams.description: A currency on a page is a promise that the card will work. Before that, establish what the payment stack supports: which currencies the gateway settles in, whether a card issued in Ghana or the UK is accepted at all, whether mobile money is available, and what the merchant of record situation is for tax. Work: one table listing each option with what the provider documents and what the billing code actually sends, then the three gaps that no document answers and who can. Deliver the capability table and the list of questions for the provider or the finance owner. No page copy until this exists.

upvotes.reason: "Find out what the billing provider can actually charge before writing any price" is a specific deliverable for this goal with a way to check it was done properly. it fills a gap the goal has open rather than restating what is already covered.
The billing provider's capabilities set the ceiling on any currency promise. Checking that first prevents a published price the checkout cannot charge.
A currency on a page is a promise the card will work; establishing what the gateway can settle before writing any foreign price is the gating fact.
A currency on a page is a promise the card will work; checking what the payment stack can actually charge first avoids publishing a price nobody can pay.
Before promising foreign-currency prices, the team needs to know what the billing provider can charge and settle. That constraint decides the whole pricing plan.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Load the pricing and sign-up pages from a foreign connection and record every currency mismatch
acceptedWorkstreams.description: A price is shown in several places on the way to paying: the card, the comparison table, the sign-up step, the billing screen. Run the whole path from outside Nigeria and record what appears at each step, including any localisation the app already attempts. Work: a step-by-step table of what a buyer sees, the currency at each step, and every place the number changes or the currency symbol is missing. Deliver the table with screenshots described in words, the list of steps that would break if the currency changed, and the one step that must be fixed first.

upvotes.reason: "Load the pricing and sign-up pages from a foreign connection and record every currency mismatch" has a scriptable structure, so it can be produced and reviewed rather than left open-ended. it fills a gap the goal has open rather than restating what is already covered.
Walking pricing to checkout from a foreign connection records the currency path and every mismatch as it is, which is the evidence any price rule needs.
Currency mismatches appear across the card, table, sign-up and billing screens; loading the flow from a foreign connection is the only way to record what a buyer actually sees.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Put currency, tax and payment in one paragraph next to the price instead of in a footnote
acceptedWorkstreams.description: Buyers outside Nigeria are not asking for a treatise; they are asking three things: what will I be charged, in what currency, and is tax included. Work: write the paragraph, decide its placement relative to the price and the button, and check it against the answer the billing screens give. Then remove or rewrite every other place on the site that touches currency, so there is one statement rather than four partial ones. Deliver the paragraph, the placement, the edited pages, and the exact wording of the invoice line it describes.

upvotes.reason: "Put currency, tax and payment in one paragraph next to the price instead of in a footnote" is a specific deliverable for this goal with a way to check it was done properly. it fills a gap the goal has open rather than restating what is already covered.
Buyers need to know what they pay, in what currency and whether tax is included; one paragraph next to the price answers all three.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Start from what the code already does: a country currency conversion exists in zedu-fe, so check it before designing a new rule
acceptedWorkstreams.description: zedu-fe already has pricing code that converts the price per country (convertedPrice with country.currencySymbol), and the billing components reference Stripe. Approach: trace where that conversion is used (public /pricing or only in-app), which countries and rates it covers and where the rate comes from, and whether checkout actually charges in that currency or only displays it. Then write the pricing-page and sign-up wording for "shown in your currency, billed in X". Done: the trace with file references, a table of what a buyer in Ghana, Kenya and the UK sees today, and the wording.

acceptedWorkstreams.title: Write what a buyer sees when their currency cannot be billed, because that is the current state
acceptedWorkstreams.description: Today a school outside Nigeria sees a naira price and no route to pay. Whatever the long-term answer, there has to be an honest path for the buyer who cannot check out. Work: design that path — what the pricing page says, where the button goes, what the contact route asks for, and what the reply promises — then test it by submitting the form as a buyer from another country and recording what happens. Deliver the copy, the route, the test result, and a note on how many enquiries a month would justify building real checkout instead.
